title: Who Owns the Themes and Taxonomy a Feedback Analytics Vendor Builds From Your Data?
summary: You own your raw comments. Who owns the derived themes and taxonomy depends on the contract. What to ask for at signing and exit, and why it matters.
body_markdown:
You signed a feedback analytics contract that says you own your data. Two years later you want to switch vendors, and you learn what "your data" covered: the raw comments. The theme structure your team spent months refining, and the record of which comment was coded to which theme, may sit outside that sentence entirely.


Who owns the themes and taxonomy? Whoever the contract says owns them, and most contracts don't say. Raw customer comments and the derived theme structure are two separate assets. The raw comments are your data, and privacy law already obliges a processor to return or delete them. The derived taxonomy and codings are a gray area. Ownership of derived data is uncertain under intellectual property law, so it's usually settled by contract. That makes the buyer's job three things: name the derived layer separately, get ownership or a perpetual license to it, and write a portable export of it in as an obligation. Thematic exports both layers today: the themes and sub-themes, and the comments with their theme assignments.


This article is informational, not legal advice. Below is what each asset is, what terms each needs, what to ask at signing and at exit, and why the derived layer is the one that decides whether you can switch vendors cleanly.


## What "themes and taxonomy" actually means


A[feedback taxonomy](https://getthematic.com/insights/how-to-build-a-customer-feedback-taxonomy) is a hierarchy of themes that brings structure to unstructured text. It's also called a code frame. In a feedback analytics platform it sits on top of your raw comments as a derived layer.


That derived layer has four parts:


- **The theme structure.** The named themes and sub-themes, such as "login issues" under "account access."
- **The codings.** The record of which comment was assigned to which theme, row by row.
- **The history.** How the structure changed over time: merges, splits, renames, and new themes.
- **The configuration.** Any rules, synonyms, or mappings your team added to tune the output.


The raw comments are the input. Everything above is output. That split matters because contracts, privacy law, and switching rules treat input and output differently.


## Why raw comments and derived themes need different terms


**Raw comments are personal data with a return obligation.** Customers put names, account numbers, and health details into free-text boxes. Under the[General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) Article 28(3)(g)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj/eng) , a processor must, "at the choice of the controller," delete or return all the personal data after the services end, and delete existing copies. That protects the comments, and Thematic has covered[analyzing feedback without mishandling personal data](https://getthematic.com/insights/gdpr-feedback-personal-data) separately. Article 28 says nothing specific about a taxonomy.


**Derived themes are the gray area.** A Practical Law practice note on[data as IP and data license agreements](https://www.friedfrank.com/uploads/siteFiles/Publications/Data%20as%20IP%20and%20Data%20License%20Agreements%20%281%29.pdf) puts it plainly: "Owing to the uncertainty of its ownership under applicable IP law, the ownership of derived data can be, and is most often, designated by and protected by contract." A vendor can reasonably argue its models and methods produced the structure. You can reasonably argue it was built from your data, by your team's refinements, for your business. The contract is where that argument gets settled.


**Switching law draws the same line.** The[EU Data Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2854/oj/eng) , which has applied since September 12, 2025, defines exportable data in Article 2(38) as the input and output data, including metadata, that the customer's use of the service generates. The same definition excludes assets or data protected by intellectual property rights. A vendor-built taxonomy is exactly the kind of output that could land on either side of that exclusion. If your contract names it as yours, or as exportable, the question goes away.


**Asset** **Default protection** **Terms to ask for**


**Raw comments** GDPR return or delete at end of service Customer owns; vendor license limited to providing the service; return format and deletion certificate


**Theme structure** Unclear; set by contract Customer owns, or holds a perpetual, royalty-free license to use after exit


**Comment-level codings** Unclear; set by contract Named as customer data or exportable data


**Theme history and configuration** Rarely addressed Named in the export specification, with a format


## Where contracts usually leave the derived layer exposed


The full set of clauses a feedback analytics agreement needs is a broader topic. For the derived layer specifically, four gaps recur:


- **"Customer Data" is defined as what you upload.** Anything the platform generates is left undefined, so its status is open to argument.
- **The vendor keeps a broad license to "usage data" or "outputs."** Read whether that covers your theme structure, and whether it survives termination.
- **Export exists as a product feature, not an obligation.** A button in the product can change. A contractual export specification cannot, without an amendment.
- **Nobody specified the format.** Themes exported as a flat list of labels lose the hierarchy. Codings exported without comment IDs can't be joined back to the source.


A quick demo-time test: ask the vendor to export your pilot's theme hierarchy and comment-level codings, then open the file. If the sub-themes are gone or the comment IDs are missing, you've learned what exit will look like.


## Why derived taxonomy portability matters when you switch vendors


The raw comments are replaceable in the sense that you usually hold a copy in your survey tool or warehouse. The derived layer is not. It encodes months of decisions about what counts as a theme, and every trend chart you've shown leadership depends on it.


Without it, a switch forces three costs:


1. **Trend breaks.** A new vendor builds a new structure, and last year's "delivery delays" may not match this year's. Leadership sees a discontinuity that's really a relabeling.
2. **Rework.** Your team re-refines a taxonomy it already refined once.
3. **Lock-in by inertia.** If the only copy of the structure lives inside the incumbent, the cost of leaving rises every quarter you stay.


Thematic's guide to[migrating a feedback history between platforms](https://getthematic.com/insights/migrate-off-medallia-qualtrics) notes that analytics tags are frequently not portable by default, and recommends mapping old code frames to the new themes during migration. That mapping is only possible if you exported the old code frame in the first place. It's the practical reason to negotiate derived-layer portability at signing rather than at exit.


## How Thematic handles the derived layer today


Thematic builds its theme taxonomy[bottom-up](https://getthematic.com/insights/inductive-thematic-analysis) from the language in your comments, as a two-level hierarchy of base themes and sub-themes. Teams refine it by adding missing themes and removing irrelevant ones.


**Thematic exports the theme structure, not just the verbatims.** Exports carry base themes alongside sub-themes, so the hierarchy survives the file. As Thematic's guide to[exporting feedback themes](https://getthematic.com/insights/export-themes-excel-powerpoint-bi) puts it: "An export that carries the raw verbatims but drops the theme structure has thrown away the analysis."


**Thematic exports comment-level codings.** The CSV of analyzed responses pairs each comment with its theme assignments, plus metadata such as scores, dates, and segments. That's the file you need to join themes against other datasets or map them into another system.


**Thematic exposes both through an API.** The API returns CSV and JSON, and theme-level data can be pushed into Snowflake, BigQuery, Tableau, Power BI, and Looker.


**Thematic re-analyzes history when a theme changes.** Thematic imports historical feedback and, when a theme changes, re-analyzes all existing feedback. That keeps trends continuous inside the platform as the structure evolves.


Those are product capabilities, not contract terms. Ownership of derived themes, license scope, termination assistance, and deletion windows belong in the agreement itself, so ask for them in writing, the same way you would with any vendor.


## What to ask for at signing and at exit


**At signing:**


1. **Who owns the derived theme structure and codings?** Look for the derived layer named separately from raw feedback.
2. **If the vendor keeps ownership, what license do we get?** Look for perpetual, royalty-free use after termination.
3. **Can the vendor reuse our theme structure for other customers or its models?** Look for a plain no, or de-identified and aggregated only.
4. **Is the export specification in the contract?** Look for theme hierarchy, comment-level codings with comment IDs, and theme history, each with a named format.
5. **For EU services, does the contract carry the Data Act switching terms?** Look for an exhaustive list of portable data and digital assets under Article 25.


**At exit:**


1. **When does the export arrive, and in what format?** The Data Act sets a maximum 30-day transitional period and a retrieval period of at least 30 days for services in scope.
2. **Is termination assistance included or billable?** Get the answer before you need it.
3. **What proof of deletion do we receive?** Look for a written certificate covering comments, codings, and backups.


## The short answer


You own your raw customer comments. Who owns the themes and taxonomy a feedback analytics vendor builds from them depends on the contract, because derived data ownership is usually set by contract rather than by law. Name the theme structure, the comment-level codings, and their history as separate assets. Get ownership or a perpetual license, and write the export format in as an obligation. One test works with any vendor, Thematic included: export your pilot's theme hierarchy and codings, and check the file before you sign.
